newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 30.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- BOCK SELLS 18 PER CENT LONRHO STAKE

Dieter Bock, the man who ousted Lonhro founder Tiny Rowland, has resigned as chief executive of the conglomerate. Bock, who has also exercised an option to sell his 18.3 per cent stake in the group, will become Lonhro's non-executive deputy chairman. The move is part of preparations for a planned demerger of Lonrho's African trading businesses. Anglo American, South Africa's biggest company, has bought Bock's stake for 257 million stg.
-- BONN SET TO MISS EMU TARGET, SAY ECONOMISTS

The autumn report from Germany's six leading economic research institutes has warned the Bonn government that the country is set to miss both the deficit and debt criteria for European economic and monetary union in 1997. The Maastricht criteria for Emu set a target for government deficit of 3 per cent of gross domestic product - but, according to the report, Germany is set to record a figure of 3.5 per cent next year. -- WATER COMPANIES RISK PRICE SQUEEZE BY REGULATOR

Water industry regulator Ofwat is to carpet some water companies to seek explanations for their apparent failure to meet spending commitments, which in turn has threatened their ability to comply with quality and environmental obligations. Ofwat has warned that some companies could be put under pressure to raise prices by less than they would be entitled to next year.
-- BANKS URGE CITY TO SCRAP PRICING IN FRACTIONS

A survey from the British Bankers Association has found support from most of the large British banks for the City of London to move to quoting market prices in decimals rather than the traditional fractions. The BBA found that it was mainly the smaller banks who would be opposed to change, largely on the basis of cost. The BBA survey will add to pressure on the City of London to embrace decimalisation ahead of European monetary union.
-- JUMP IN CONSUMER BORROWING ADDS TO PRESSURE FOR RATE RISE

Figures from the Bank of England have revealed that consumers borrowed a seasonally adjusted 1.1 bn stg in September, the third successive month that borrowing has exceeded 1 bn sterling. The news will add to pressure on chancellor Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates, coming as it does at the same time as a warning from Martin Weale, one of his independent advisors, that the government is no longer on course to hit its inflation target.
-- PENSIONS PROBE TOO SLOW SAYS REPORT

The second annual report from an independent consumer group set up to review the work of city watchdog the Personal Investment Authority has warned that the PIA's review into the mis-selling of personal pensions was 'unacceptably slow' and is damaging consumer confidence. The mis-selling review was set up by the Securities and Investments Board in 1994, and the panel urged the PIA to do everything it could to speed up progress.
-- MORGAN GRENFELL TROUBLES HIT UNIT TRUST INVESTMENT

Figures published Tuesday by the Association of Unit Trusts and Investment Funds show that net investments in unit trusts by private investors fell in September to 205 million stg, compared to 347m stg in August. The fall has been attributed to unease caused by the suspension by Morgan Grenfell of three unit trusts and the sacking of star fund manager Peter Young.
-- HOLLYWOOD AGREES DEAL ON DIGITAL VIDEO DISCS

The Hollywood film industry has reached provisional agreement with the consumer electronics industry over copyright protection for the new digital video disc (DVC) format. DVC has been seen as the next generation of compact disc technology, capable of storing digital versions of feature-length films. DVC hardware had been due to go on sale in the summer, but was delayed because of the copyright problems. Matsushita is to launch DVC players on the Japanese market next month, but Sony is expected to wait until the Spring.
-- CIDER GROUP PLAN HALTS SHARE SLIDE

Troubled cider producer Matthew Clark, which has seen its share price halved in the past six weeks, has announced details of its recovery plan. The group has been hit severely by competition from the new 'alcopops', and plans to hit back by increasing its sales and marketing staff for branded drinks from 170 to 210. News of the recovery plan and the group's intention to maintain its interim dividend saw shares rise slightly to close up 17p at 317.5p.
-- ERICSSON CLAIMS LEAD AS PRE-TAX JUMPS 23 PER CENT

Swedish telecommunications equipment maker Ericsson has reported a 23.4 per cent increase in third quarter pre-tax profits, to SKr2.148 bn (203 million stg). The group now claims to be the world's largest supplier of mobile and fixed-network systems after reporting 20 consecutive quarters of improved order bookings. Shares in Ericsson fell by more than 3 per cent on the news, due to profit-taking, but shares in Scandinvian rival Nokia fell by almost 4 per cent as dealers concluded that Ericsson may be taking a larger share of Nokia's core markets.
